samples.scenario: A mid-level manager receives an email apparently from the CEO requesting immediate access to confidential HR files. The email originates from a domain similar to the corporate domain but with a swapped letter, bypassing SPF but failing DKIM and DMARC due to incomplete DNS records. The attacker includes a link to a fake SharePoint login page designed to capture credentials.

samples.scenario: An employee in the HR department receives an email impersonating the CEO requesting confidential employee salary data for an alleged external audit. The attacker uses a homoglyph domain exploiting Cyrillic characters similar to the legitimate domain and sends the email from an IP address not authorized in SPF records. DKIM signature is missing, and DMARC policy is set to quarantine but not enforced strictly due to reporting-only mode. The email instructs the employee to upload files via a shared cloud link hosted on a domain mimicking a popular cloud storage provider.

samples.scenario: A finance team member receives an email allegedly from the VP of Finance requesting immediate payment of an outstanding invoice to a new vendor. The email domain is a lookalike domain using a subdomain of a free mail service combined with the legitimate company domain, and the sender IP is from a public cloud provider. SPF passes because the attacker uses a compromised cloud mail server, but DKIM signature fails due to domain mismatch. The email contains a link to a fake invoice hosted on a compromised but legitimate third-party vendor website.
